title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives and Runbooks (Comprehensive Guidance)
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE guidance for defining and operating SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbooks. It is intended for oncall SREs, platform engineers, and service owners who must set measurable reliability targets and operational procedures for production services.

Goals
- Provide a standard SLO / error budget framework that balances developer velocity and customer-facing reliability.
- Define capacity planning practices to maintain SLOs at expected traffic growth and failure modes.
- Capture runbook templates and escalation procedures for common classes of incidents.
- Standardize post-incident review (PIR) and reliability initiative processes to reduce recurrence.
- List operational tooling, dashboards, and automations SREs should rely on.

Scope and ownership
- Scope: All externally-facing inference endpoints, control-plane services that affect latency or availability (routing, auth, model catalog), and internal critical infra (GPU scheduler, KV cache).
- Service owner: Product/Platform teams are responsible for proposing SLOs. SRE reviews and approves. Final SLO and runbook ownership is recorded in the service registry.

SLO and error budget framework
1) SLO types (choose the set that best maps to the service):
   - Availability SLO: percentage of successful user requests per rolling 30d window (e.g., 99.95%).
   - Latency SLOs: percentile-based response time targets per API surface (p50, p95, p99).
   - Correctness/Quality SLOs: for model-driven endpoints, a quality metric (e.g., BLEU, accuracy on canonical prompt sets) tied to regressions.
   - Throughput SLO: sustained RPS or tokens/sec for dedicated capacity customers.

2) Example target values (guideline only; service owners must justify alternatives):
   - Hosted inference (api.redwood.ai/generate): Availability 99.95% (30d), p95 latency < 300ms for text generation baseline model at 512 context length.
   - Dedicated capacity control-plane: Availability 99.9% (30d).
   - Model catalog operations: Availability 99.99% for reads, 99.9% for writes.

3) Error budget calculation
   - Error budget = (1 - SLO) * measurement window. E.g., for 99.95% over 30 days: allowed downtime = 0.05% * 30 days = ~21.6 minutes.
   - Error budget burn measured by: failed requests (HTTP 5xx, non-2xx business-level failures), latency breaches for latency SLOs, and quality regression triggers for correctness SLOs.

4) Burn policies and guardrails
   - Green: <50% budget used — normal operations.
   - Yellow: 50–80% used — inform owners; freeze non-critical releases; prioritize reliability fixes.
   - Red: >80% used — immediate moratorium on feature releases that touch the service, mandatory incident review and mitigation plan submitted within 24 hours, and capacity / scaling steps executed per runbook.

5) Emergency throttle policy
   - If error budget in a 24-hour window exceeds 20% (fast burn), trigger autoscale + throttling of best-effort routes and non-critical tenants. SRE lead must be paged.

Defining SLOs for model-driven systems
- For endpoints where the model output quality is critical, define baseline prompt sets and metrics (e.g., BLEU / ROUGE / domain-specific accuracy). Run automated evaluations daily in the eval-harness.
- Quality regressions that reduce metric beyond agreed threshold (e.g., absolute drop >1.5% on critical prompt set) count as SLO breach and consume error budget until mitigated.

Capacity planning and operational capacity model
1) Capacity model components
   - Baseline capacity (N): number of GPU seats, inference workers, and routing frontends required to meet p95 latency at expected peak traffic with safety margin.
   - Headroom factor: typically 25% for hosted API, 50% for dedicated bursts depending on SLA.
   - Failure domain redundancy: at least 2 availability zones per region; cross-region failover for enterprise-critical tenants.

2) Planning cadence
   - Monthly: review usage trends, forecast next 90 days using 3% weekly growth or applied customer commit information.
   - Quarterly: capacity review with sales for Dedicated bookings and upcoming model launches.
   - Pre-Launch: run load tests and synthetic traffic tests for any significant model or config change (see Runbooks).

3) Capacity thresholds and automated actions
   - Warning: 65% sustained utilization on any GPU pool for >30 minutes — create scaling ticket to increase reserved capacity or enable burst; notify owners.
   - Elevated: 85% sustained utilization — trigger autoscaling policies and relocate low-priority workloads to on-demand/spot pools.
   - Critical: 95% utilization or OOMs observed — throttle non-critical tenants, enable emergency burst, page SRE.

4) Autoscaling guidance
   - Use queue length (requests/sec waiting), GPU memory headroom, and average token-generation throughput as primary signals. Prefer predictive scaling combined with reactive scale-up.

Operational tooling and dashboards
- Monitoring: Prometheus + Cortex for long-term metrics storage. Key metrics: request rate, error rate, p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, avg tokens/sec, KV cache hit rate, grace-fallback rate.
- Tracing: Jaeger for distributed traces with sampling policy aligned to p99 tail and anomalous traces.
- Alerting: Alertmanager rules map to runbook severity levels (SEV1/SEV2/SEV3).
- Incident management: PagerDuty for paging, Slack for incident channels, Confluence for post-incident reports.
- Tooling integrations: CI pipelines for runbook tests, canary deploy platform, and chaos-testing harness (chaos-engine) for reliability exercises.

Runbooks (templates and examples)
- Runbook structure (every runbook must include the following sections):
  1) Title and service identifier (service-slug)
  2) Summary/impact (what user-visible symptoms look like)
  3) Pager escalation matrix (roles, contact methods)
  4) Immediate mitigation steps (ordered bullets)
  5) Diagnostic commands and dashboards (copyable commands)
  6) Post-incident actions and owner assignments
  7) Links to related docs and previous incidents

- Example: SEV1: Hosted API 5xx spike runbook (abridged)
  Summary: Sudden increase in 5xx responses for /v1/generate endpoints affecting >5% of traffic.
  Pager: SEV1 to SRE oncall -> SRE manager if not acknowledged in 5 minutes.
  Immediate mitigation steps:
    1) Confirm scope: query error-rate dashboard: 
       curl -s "https://metrics/api/query?query=rate(http_requests_total{job=hosted_api,status=5xx}[5m])"
    2) If errors originate from a single model shard pool, route traffic away by updating routing policy: 
       curl -X POST https://controlplane/api/v1/routing -d '{"rule":"route-away","target":"fallback-model"}'
    3) Scale up target worker pool by +25% (or enable burst):
       kubectl patch hpa hosted-api -p '{"spec":{"replicas":X}}' # replace X accordingly
    4) If CPU/GPU OOMs observed, reduce batch size and restart problematic workers.
  Diagnostics:
    - Check worker logs: kubectl logs -lapp=hosted-api-worker --since=15m
    - Trace tail-sampled requests in Jaeger with tag service=hosted-api
  Recovery and post-incident:
    - Restore routing after fix; run synthetic regression tests; file PIR within 48 hours.

Incident review standards (PIR)
- Timeline: PIR draft due within 48 hours; final PIR published within 7 days.
- PIR must include: summary, impact (users affected, downtime minutes, error budget consumption), timeline of events, root cause analysis (RCA), why mitigations failed/why not, action items with owners and due dates, regressions to SLOs, and monitoring gaps.
- Severity-to-PIR mapping: all SEV1s require a full PIR; SEV2s require a short-form PIR if >2 hours customer impact.
- Action items: categorise as short-term (<=2 weeks), medium (<=90 days), long-term (>90 days) and track in the reliability initiatives backlog.

Reliability initiatives and roadmap
- Initiative intake: any engineer can propose a reliability initiative via the reliability backlog template. Initiative must include hypothesis, measurement plan, and acceptance criteria (improvement to SLO or reduction in error budget burn).
- Prioritization: SRE roadmap planning session (monthly) ranks initiatives based on customer impact, error budget savings, and implementation effort.
- Example initiatives:
  - Prefix/KV cache: reduce tail latency by enabling multi-tenant KV caching with warm-cache population (expected p99 improvement 20%).
  - Autoscaler improvements: predictive scaling on model popularity signals to reduce scale-up time by 40%.
  - Tracing sampling improvements: targeted tail-sampling for long-running inference chains to improve RCA signal.

Playbook for onboarding a new service
1) Service owner proposes SLOs, baseline model metrics, and traffic patterns.
2) SRE review: confirm SLO measurability and instrumentation.
3) Create runbook and test by running tabletop exercises/gamedays.
4) Add dashboards and alerts to monitoring tenant and link to runbook.
5) Record final SLO and runbook in the service registry and schedule quarterly reviews.

Documentation and templates (links)
- Runbook template: /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-template (use the runbook structure above)
- PIR template: /confluence/eng-sre/pir-template
- Capacity workbook: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning-workbook
- Eval harness integration: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness

Appendices
A) Useful queries and commands (examples)
- Check P95 latency for hosted API:
  prometheus query: "histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=hosted_api}[5m])) by (le))"
- Check GPU pool utilization (Cortex metrics):
  curl -s 'https://metrics/api/query?query=avg_over_time(gpu_utilization_percent{pool="inference-pool"}[10m])'

B) Runbook severity mapping
- SEV1: Partial or total service outage impacting many customers or >10% of requests. Requires immediate paging and full PIR.
- SEV2: Degraded service impacting smaller subset or increased latency beyond SLO for >30 minutes. Requires oncall intervention and short PIR if significant.
- SEV3: Minor impact, single-customer issue, or non-production impact. Documented and tracked but no mandatory PIR.

C) Contact matrix
